title: When Scrolling Stops Being a Habit
hook: Losing sleep to your phone isn't automatically an addiction — but there's a line, and courts are now arguing over who put it there.
key_points: Claims that Meta deliberately engineered its platforms to be addictive are being tested in court.
A bad habit and an addiction aren't the same thing — the difference is loss of control, not hours logged.
Warning signs include scrolling instead of sleeping, and failing to stop even when you want to.
Nighttime use is a common tipping point: it eats the sleep that would otherwise protect your mood.
The practical fix is changing what the phone can do at night, not relying on willpower alone.
content_html: If you keep meaning to sleep and end up scrolling instead, you're in familiar company — and, per NPR, the question of whether that's your fault or the app's design is now being argued in court, where claims that Meta deliberately made its platforms addictive are being tested.
extra_html:
NPR's reporting draws the line where clinicians do: a bad habit is something you'd rather do less of, while an addiction is something you can't stop doing even when it's clearly costing you. Hours logged is a weak signal on its own. The stronger signals are loss of control and the price you pay — most commonly, sleep you meant to get.

That's also where the practical advice points. Rather than white-knuckling it, change what the phone is able to do at the hours you're most vulnerable: charge it out of the bedroom, cut off the feeds that pull you back, and make the default action at midnight something other than opening an app.

related.title: Building Healthier Screen Habits
related.hook: You don't need to quit your phone — just out-design it. A few small tweaks beat willpower for taking back your attention.

related.title: Screens and Your Wellbeing
related.hook: It's not just how many hours you're on a screen — it's how and when. The same phone can leave you rested or wrecked depending on use.

related.title: Building Better Sleep Habits
related.hook: Good sleep is mostly built in the hours before bed. A handful of simple habits — collectively called sleep hygiene — do more than any gadget.

flashcards.prompt: What separates a bad scrolling habit from something closer to an addiction?
flashcards.back_html: Not the raw hour count — it's loss of control: you keep scrolling even when you want to stop, and it starts costing you things like sleep.

flashcards.prompt: Why is nighttime scrolling singled out as a warning sign?

choices.text: It displaces sleep, which otherwise protects mood and functioning
Screens emit radiation that is dangerous after dark
Apps are technically more addictive after midnight

flashcards.explanation_html: Scrolling instead of sleeping is the flagged pattern: the cost lands on sleep, which is what keeps mood and daily functioning steady.

flashcards.prompt: What is currently being tested in court about social platforms?
flashcards.back_html: Claims that Meta deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive — moving the question from personal willpower to product design.
